analysis.one_liner: Repeals tax breaks and royalty relief for oil and gas companies and tightens their foreign tax rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 27, 2006 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never received a markup or a vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take back a long list of federal giveaways to the oil and gas industry: it would end the deduction for intangible drilling and development costs, the percentage depletion allowance, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and roughly ten provisions of the 2005 energy law that reduced royalties or gave tax breaks for drilling, deepwater production, pipelines, refineries, and transmission lines. It would also require very large integrated oil companies to revalue their crude oil inventories for tax purposes and would narrow the foreign tax credits available to oil companies operating abroad. The revenue raised would go back to the Treasury; the bill did not attach it to any new spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would collect the revenue now spent on oil and gas tax deductions, credits, and royalty relief; and, indirectly, consumers and communities whose energy policy would no longer subsidize oil and gas production while gasoline and heating prices were high.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the deduction for intangible drilling and development costs, the percentage depletion allowance for oil and gas wells, and the credit for enhanced oil recovery costs, three long-standing tax benefits for oil and gas producers [S2][S3].

Repeals provisions of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 that gave the industry royalty relief, production incentives, deepwater royalty suspension, Alaska offshore royalty suspension, and accelerated depreciation for refineries, pipelines, and transmission property [S2][S3].

Requires integrated oil companies producing at least 500,000 barrels of crude per day, with over $1 billion in gross receipts, to revalue their LIFO crude and petroleum inventories at $18.75 per barrel, raising their taxable income [S3].

Limits foreign tax credits for 'dual capacity' taxpayers (companies receiving economic benefits from foreign governments in exchange for their payments) and eliminates deferral of foreign oil and gas extraction income, ending tax shelters available to companies drilling abroad [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, especially the largest integrated producers, would pay more in taxes and lose royalty relief; their investors would absorb the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and investors

drawbacks.text: Ending the intangible drilling cost deduction and depletion allowance would raise the cost of drilling a well, and the industry's good-faith argument is that higher after-tax drilling costs mean less domestic exploration and production, which could tighten supply and raise prices for consumers [S2][S3].

The bill is a pure revenue raiser with no provision directing the money to consumers, low-income energy assistance, or cleaner energy, so its benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on how the Treasury uses or forgives the funds [S2][S3].

The LIFO revaluation formula at a fixed $18.75 per barrel is a one-time penalty targeted at specific large companies rather than a general tax rule, an approach critics could fairly call punitive and retroactive in style [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax breaks and royalty relief being repealed are genuine public costs at a time of high energy prices, and ending them would put real money back in federal hands. The honest counterweights are real: some of the repealed provisions were designed to encourage domestic production, and the bill attaches the recovered revenue to nothing that directly helps consumers. On balance the bill shifts money from a highly profitable, highly subsidized industry back to taxpayers, and its main flaw is design, not intent.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever followed, so it died when the Congress ended [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Senator John Kerry introduced the bill on April 27, 2006, during a period of high gasoline prices, with Senator Reid introducing it on his behalf along with Senators Kohl and Lieberman [S3][S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, especially large integrated companies, kept every deduction, credit, and royalty relief the bill would have repealed, and the Treasury kept spending nothing new on consumers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers kept their tax breaks

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it, and it never reached a vote, so the record shows Democratic sponsorship but only inferred opposition from the committee's inaction [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would end the intangible drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and several 2005-law royalty and production incentives, so producers would owe more tax and lose royalty relief they currently keep. Their interest in keeping these breaks runs directly against the public's interest in recovering the subsidy cost.

Companies producing 500,000+ barrels a day with over $1 billion in receipts would be forced to revalue their LIFO inventories at $18.75 per barrel, increasing taxable income, and would face tighter foreign tax credit rules. This is the bill's most targeted provision, aimed squarely at the biggest firms.

industries.industry: Electric transmission and natural gas distribution utilities
industries.note: The bill would terminate early 15-year and 7-year depreciation treatment for electric transmission property, natural gas distribution lines, and gathering lines, which raises these companies' near-term tax bills. The public effect is less clear-cut: the tax breaks were meant to spur infrastructure investment that also benefits consumers.

The bill would cut off expensing for refinery property and end the small refiner exception to oil depletion limits, raising refiners' tax costs. Repealing a refinery incentive during a period of tight fuel supply could work against consumers, though it also removes a subsidy to a profitable industry.
Two-year amortization of geological and geophysical expenditures would end, making exploration surveying more expensive and potentially slowing new discovery work.
